extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, translators, poets, public speakers, and teachers of literature (early-18th-century literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical critical advice on translating lyric poetry, performing and teaching rhetoric, and literary pedagogy: assesses what makes a good poetic translation, effective oratory, stage practice, and methods for cultivating taste in youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation fidelity: word-for-word and short turn of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: “the three first Stanzas are rendred almost Word for Word, and not only with the same Elegance, but with the same short Turn of Expression which is so remarkable in the Greek, and so peculiar to the Sapphick Ode.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer translations that preserve the original's concision and characteristic turns of phrase; compare candidate translations directly with the original to judge closeness of wording and stylistic economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the passion/vehemence of the original
rubrics_metrics.description: “Monsieur Boileau has given us all the Poetry, but not all the Passion of this famous Fragment...the Circumstances do not lie so thick together, and follow one another with that Vehemence and Emotion as in the Original.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good translation should recreate not only poetic language but the intensity and sequence of emotional impulses; avoid smoothing or diluting rapid, piled-up circumstances that create the original's force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture the spirit of the original within language limits
rubrics_metrics.description: “This Translation is written in the very Spirit of Sappho, and as near the Greek as the Genius of our Language will possibly suffer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to render the 'spirit' or genius of the source text while respecting natural idiom of the target language; accept necessary adaptations imposed by linguistic differences but keep the original's tone and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism/naturalism in emotional description (an 'exact Copy of Nature')
rubrics_metrics.description: “Longinus has observed, that this Description of Love in Sappho is an exact Copy of Nature...all the Circumstances which follow one another in such an Hurry of Sentiments...are really such as happen in the Phrenzies of Love.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow apparently contradictory or extreme images if they faithfully reflect actual human experience; faithful depiction of complex, rapid emotions increases credibility and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and compactness characteristic of lyric form
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for the Sapphick 'short Turn of Expression' indicates value placed on concise, tightly-turned phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In translating or composing lyric verse, favor concise, concentrated expression that mirrors the compressed energy of the original form rather than expansive paraphrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty as a rhetorical and performative virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: “a just and reasonable Modesty does not only recommend Eloquence...Modest Merit has a double Claim to Acceptance...Cicero tells us that he never liked an Orator who did not appear in some little Confusion at the Beginning of his Speech.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For speakers and performers, modesty (a degree of timidity or concern at outset) enhances audience goodwill; confident insolence is less appealing—cultivate modest demeanor without undermining competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical clarity and control of speech ('organs of speech')
rubrics_metrics.description: “the several Organs of Speech which an Orator ought to have in Perfection, as the Tongue, the Teeth [the Lips,] the Nose, the Palate, and the Wind-pipe...the most material Organ...the Forehead.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to vocal technique and the bodily means of articulation (pronunciation, breath control, posture/forehead as expressive control); consider devices (metaphorical or literal) to check excessive volume or poor delivery (e.g., a 'hush-note' to check long stories, swearing, obscenity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ridicule/satire to correct sentimental extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ridicule, perhaps, is a better Expedient against Love than sober Advice...Hudibras and Don Quixote may be as effectual to cure the Extravagancies of this Passion, as any of the old Philosophers.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ satire and comic treatment as an effective literary strategy to moderate or expose excessive sentimentality; mockery can function as therapeutic or corrective rhetoric in subject-matter treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogy for cultivating literary taste and language skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to instruct youth with polite entertainments and classical reading: teach music, dancing, drawing; introduce best English writers; make themselves Masters of the Latin Tongue; exercise Style in Writing light Pieces frequently in their Native Language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate taste by combining pleasurable accomplishments with guided reading of exemplary writers, regular composition practice in the native tongue, recitation/acting exercises, and gradual introduction to Latin and classical authors; emphasize forming taste before rigorous analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging and role-assignment to manage performer nerves
rubrics_metrics.description: “It would not be amiss, if such an one were at first introduced as a Ghost or a Statue, till he recovered his Spirits, and grew fit for some living Part.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing inexperienced or nervous performers, assign roles or staging that reduce pressure (non-speaking or less exposed parts) as transitional steps toward full performance; use practical staging to build confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational prudence regarding 'inquisitive' interlocutors
rubrics_metrics.description: “there is nothing, methinks, so dangerous as to communicate Secrets to them; for the same Temper of Enquiry makes them as impertinently communicative...They are the Channels through which all the Good and Evil that is spoken in Town are conveyed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat highly inquisitive, talkative persons as unreliable custodians of confidential material; either avoid sharing secrets with them or deliberately use them to disseminate information, knowing they will pass it on.
